bio.en: Nikhyl Singhal is a veteran product executive who spent years at Meta and Google, served as CPO of Credit Karma, founded four companies, and now leads the leading communities for heads of product (Skip).
bio.zh: Nikhyl Singhal 是一位资深产品高管，曾长期任职于 Meta 和 Google，担任过 Credit Karma 的 CPO，是四家公司的创始人，如今运营着面向产品负责人与 CPO 的顶尖社区 Skip。

summary.en: Nikhyl argues that AI is radically reshaping product management, with information-movers being displaced by builders who can ship quickly. He predicts a near-term wave of layoffs followed by rehiring of AI-first talent, and stresses that PMs must develop judgment, pace, and hands-on building skills to stay relevant. The episode reframes career advice around becoming a builder rather than a coordinator.
summary.zh: Nikhyl 认为，在 AI 的冲击下，产品管理的角色正在被彻底重塑，单纯传递信息的“信息搬运工”将被能够亲手快速构建产品的“建造者”取代。他预测短期内会出现大规模裁员，随后企业会以 AI 优先的方式重新招人，并强调产品经理必须培养判断力、节奏感和动手构建的能力才能保持竞争力。本期将职业建议重新定义为：成为建造者，而非协调者。

turns.zh: 行业变革即将拉开帷幕。我们的行业正深陷压力之中。没有什么是永恒不变的。每个人都处于高度戒备状态。如果你三年前与产品负责人交谈，他们的一天主要就是传递信息。但信息搬运工注定会成为历史。

或许我该从这里开始。我记得我们最初聊天时，大概是在新冠疫情结束后不久，当时我们所说的"零利率政策时代"——即投资者提供的零利率免费资金——正达到顶峰。我们探讨了集成电路（ICs）如今日益走俏的趋势，也谈到了首轮裁员浪潮的兴起，指出许多初创公司正面临挑战。但若你回想三年前那些深陷困境的产品经理，他们的日子可谓苦不堪言。我的意思是，他们每天的工作主要就是将信息从一个部门传递到另一个部门。（00:04:47）：那个职能部门逐渐沦为"有责无权"的状态。这是职场压力的最极端形式。如今我们不谈这些，只谈当下种种压力。比如，人工智能会取代我们的职能部门等等。但说实话，如果你回想一下自己在产品领域的过往岁月，那才是艰难的时期。当时薪资丰厚，裁员才刚刚开始，整个行业规模空前。产品经理和首席产品官的数量创下历史新高。如今的变化在于，人们又找回了乐趣，尤其是在产品领域——因为他们能亲手打造产品，不再依赖他人来实现价值。（00:05:38）：他们的创意与客户需求之间的直接联系更加紧密，也能更自由地测试产品直觉。某种程度上，这对产品行业来说是一场全面复兴。在我所在的团队中，许多顶尖的产品建设者如今薪资达到了历史高点，收到的offer比以往任何时候都多，他们可能成为创始人、CEO，或是转向非产品职位，但至少会担任C级高管。他们感觉前所未有的机遇触手可及，这确实是好消息。但说实话，这背后也隐藏着诸多隐忧。首先是精疲力竭。我从未见过哪个行业比现在更疲惫。（00:06:38）：新冠期间我们也疲惫不堪，但原因不同。过去，掌握了本职技能后，你就能安稳工作十年；成为管理者后，再安稳十年；成为高管后，又能安稳十年。而如今，若三个月内不提升技能，他们就会质问："你还在做那个事？三个月前我们就不这么做了。PRD？那根本就不是……"一切都让人如坐针毡。此外，现在听说大厂裁员数万人，同时又在开出三倍薪资的招聘广告。这令人难以置信，但不同立场的人对此看法迥异。（00:07:32）：我认为许多处于职业生涯中期的人——比如30多岁的职场人士——正面临残酷的现实：你事业上最具活力与精力的阶段恰恰与安定下来相重叠——因为这时你终于找到了自己的定位。但与此同时，你可能要面对养育子女、父母老去的现实，身体也开始出现各种毛病。你不得不考虑饮食健康，不能再每天吃饼干，还得锻炼身体。
你的健康状况、那些难得一见的亲友、父母——如今你不得不与他们建立全新的关系，他们正变得越来越依赖你；还有你与孩子的亲子关系。（00:08:23）然后，顺便说一句，你的工作会占据你所有空闲时间，而且需求总在变化。这一代人历来承受着巨大的压力。如今我们却像这样：“嘿，别睡了，CloudCo又有新变化了！他们今早又改了设计。” 这让人头晕目眩。我觉得这其中有快乐，但也有一种前所未见的疲惫感。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, I had this meetup last Thursday and it was a fun meetup. I have a group of about 125 heads of products, and we tend to gather once a month in San Francisco. During this meetup, we took an approach where lots of people were building things for their own companies or on their own to help themselves with productivity. We said, "Hey, why don't we do a show and tell? Why don't we just have you, if you're a head of product, just show things that are interesting, that are worth explaining." We had a startup go up and show what they're doing, and then we had some insights companies and some late stage companies. It was a few things that were really palpable. One was, there was so much joy in the audience that people were like, "Oh, I've been building this thing and let me show you." (00:12:58): Everyone had their laptop and they were one-upping each other and they were like, "Your chief of staff does that. My chief of staff does this thing." That builds on my point that people are having fun being hands-on. But the second thing is that the way they talk about how product decisions are made, the way they talked about how prioritization is determined, the way they talked about how information moves within the company, looked like a completely foreign animal from anything that I had experienced when I was working a few years back. I got up on stage and I said, "If you think about how we work right now and how you folks are all talking about using agents in your enterprise, how you're using chief of staff apps to essentially drive more productivity. (00:13:50): How all of you are essentially spending all your time just focusing on judgment and you're spending all your time taking anything that can be obsoleted and writing software around it." I think none of that was even in the language, even in the vernacular 12 months ago. Now, what is it going to look like in 12 months? Everyone had a pause and they're like, "Yeah, it was impossible to anticipate what this conversation would look like 12 months ago." It's pretty hard to understand where things are going. But I would say, I think maybe I'll answer your question around where things are going in the next couple years based on how I think companies are going to change and how people are going to change. (00:14:34): I think on the company side, I think that, and then maybe I'll slant it more towards product for a second. Product leaders will increasingly get paid and be asked to drive judgment, and then be the tip of the sphere on trying to essentially obsolete everything else through software, through AI, through agents. This is partly why there's a lot of excitement, because just to be very honest with you and you were a PM and I was a PM, most of the stuff that you didn't like doing are the things that AI is really taking a real crack at. I think that's super interesting. I think that there's a ton of that change that's going to happen. Some companies are doing it now, some companies will do it, but within two years I think most of these companies will obsolete all the mechanical parts of building product. (00:15:29): I think that there will be 10 to a hundred times more changes that will be presented to products than ever before, because now the cost of testing something, the cost of changing is going to be much, much lower. When things are changing that rapidly, that judgment piece becomes pretty much paramount.
turns.zh: 是的，我上周四参加了那次聚会，很有意思。我们这个由约125位产品负责人组成的团体，每月都会在旧金山聚会。这次聚会的形式是让大家分享自己为公司或个人开发的工具，以提升工作效率。我们提议：“何不来一场展示与分享会呢？如果你是产品负责人，何不向大家展示那些有趣且值得解释的成果呢？” 首先，一家初创公司上台演示他们的产品，随后还有几家成长期公司和成熟期公司发言。其中有几个点非常明显。其一，观众们兴致勃勃，纷纷主动上台展示自己的成果。（00:12:58）：每个人都打开笔记本电脑，互相攀比，说：“你的首席助理也能做到这个？我的首席助理能做那个！” 这恰恰印证了我的观点，即人们乐于亲自参与实践。但更重要的是，他们谈论产品决策制定方式、优先级确定流程，以及信息在公司内部的流转方式时，所使用的术语和表述方式，与我几年前的工作经历完全不同。我上台后问道：“看看我们现在的工作方式，再看看你们在谈论如何在企业中应用智能助手，通过首席助理应用提升生产力。（00:13:50）你们所有人都把时间花在做判断上，把能被淘汰的功能写成软件。” 12个月前，这些概念甚至不在我们的日常用语之列。再过12个月会怎样呢？大家都陷入沉默，说：“是啊，要预测12个月前的对话内容实在太难了。” 当下很难预测未来走向。但我可以根据对企业和人才变革的观察，谈谈未来几年的趋势。（00:14:34）：在企业层面，我认为产品负责人将越来越被重视，他们需要具备判断能力，并通过软件、AI和智能助手来淘汰传统流程。这正是当前令人兴奋的原因。说实话，你曾是产品经理，我也曾是产品经理，大多数我们不喜欢的重复性工作，如今都由AI接手了。这太有趣了。未来两年，大部分公司都将淘汰产品开发中的机械性环节。（00:15:29）：产品迭代的频率将比以往高出10到100倍，因为测试和改进成本将大幅降低。当变化如此迅速时，判断力将成为核心竞争力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make sure we understand, when you say judgment, what should people be thinking of when you talk about judgment?
turns.zh: 先确认一下理解，当你提到“判断”时，人们应该怎么理解这个词？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I think that it's evaluating whether the thing that we're changing is a good or bad thing. I think that it's also evaluating whether we should change the product in one way versus another. You can't build a hundred custom versions of the same product. It affects your brand, it affects the maintainability, et cetera. When customers are asking for things, when you're trying to think through how do you build something that's sustainable, differentiated, that's judgment. Evaluating whether it's successfully met that criteria and whether it's worth building and worth releasing, it's almost like the system skill that's existed from the beginning of the internet. It's, "Hey, it's not about the feature, it's around the system that we're putting together, the platform, if you will, that's enabling capability." (00:16:47): That's the judgment of, boy, there's all these changes coming in. They're going to happen more frequently. As an aside, because of all these changes, I think that in two years, I think there won't be any more bad software. This is maybe more of a wish and a dream than a prediction, but I think that if you count in the week, in your given week, how much bad software you come back with. I have a house and it has 15 different apps that run to control everything from the shades, to the air conditioner, to the garage door. Almost every one of those apps are afforded. They don't work particularly well. They never get monitored. Things break, no one ever checks it. (00:17:32): All that stuff's going to get fixed because someone's going to basically sit down and tell Claude to fix it, and it's just going to fix it. It's going to fix it. It's going to be more secure, et cetera. I think that that's changing, and so people will have a lot less tolerance for bad software.
turns.zh: 我认为这是在评估我们所做的改变是好是坏。同时也在评估我们是否应该以某种方式去改进产品。你不可能为同一个产品打造一百个定制版本。这会影响品牌形象，降低可维护性等等。当客户提出需求时，当你试图思考如何打造一个可持续、差异化的产品时，这就是判断。评估它是否成功达到了这些标准，是否值得去开发和发布，这几乎就像互联网诞生以来就存在的系统技能。它是，“嘿，重点不在于功能，而在于我们正在搭建的系统，平台，如果你愿意，可以称之为赋能能力。”（00:16:47）：这就是判断——天哪，有这么多变化即将到来。它们会越来越频繁地发生。顺便说一句，由于这些变化，我认为两年内就不会再有糟糕的软件了。这可能更多是愿望和梦想，而非预测，但我认为如果你计算一下，在给定的一周里，你遇到多少糟糕的软件。我有一栋房子，里面有15个不同的应用程序，用于控制从窗帘、空调到车库门的所有设备。几乎每个应用程序都漏洞百出，根本没有监控。东西坏了，也没人去检查。（00:17:32）：所有这些问题都会得到解决，因为有人会坐下来，告诉Claude去修复它，然后它就会修复。它会修复。它会更安全等等。这些都在发生变化，所以人们对糟糕的软件将越来越不容忍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, just real quick at a quick aside to your side, the prompt I constantly find myself using with Codex and Claude is just how can we make the product experience better? How can we make this better? You just ask that and it's like, "Here's 10 ways we can make it better." It's like, "Wow, these are really good ideas." Then cool, do the first seven.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我经常对Codex和Claude使用的一个提示就是，如何让产品体验更好。你只要问这个问题，就会得到10种改进方法。然后你会惊叹，“哇，这些想法真不错。”接着选前七个实施。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Exactly. There's going to be some super skill that's going to run against every piece of software that's in the App Store, and it's going to basically go in and it's going to fix them all. Then they're going to get released and they're going to be like, "Oh, it's just a significantly more consistent, better, less buggy experience and more maintainable." That's why there's a lot of optimism because these changes can be done pretty automatically.
turns.zh: 没错。会有一种超级技能，针对App Store里的每款软件运行，它会自动修复所有问题。然后这些软件发布后，人们会说：“哦，体验明显更稳定、更流畅、更少漏洞，也更易于维护了。” 这就是为什么人们如此乐观，因为这些改进可以相当自动化地完成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's easy to, just to finish that loop real quick, so many of these apps are built by engineers that are not the best engineers. They're engineers that companies hire that don't really care about their software. They're just like, "This is just a side thing building this thing that we have just app. We just need to build an app. Let's find someone to build it." They're not like product first companies. Now, all of these companies have access to the most skilled software engineer, Cloud Code, Codex and all these other tools. I totally see what you're saying. Everyone has the best engineers available now, and it's just English to ask them to build the better thing or build a better app. That's a really interesting point.
turns.zh: 是啊。这其实挺简单的，只要快速完成那个循环就行。很多这类应用都是由并非最顶尖的工程师开发的。他们是公司雇佣的工程师，根本不把软件质量当回事。他们只会说：“这只是顺便开发的一个应用，我们需要尽快上线，就随便找个人做吧。”这些公司根本不以产品为先。如今所有公司都能接触到最优秀的软件工程师，Cloud Code、Codex等工具也唾手可得。我完全明白你的意思。现在每个人都能找到顶尖工程师，只要让他们开发更好的产品或应用就行了。这真是个很有意思的观点。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: It still boggles my mind. Everyone's like, "Oh, what's the cutting edge and all of that." I think there's still, I don't know if this is true even today, but very recently there were more lines of Cobalt than I think any other language out there. Mainframe sales continue to do pretty well and they're unusually large line item for companies like IBM. Part of the reason why these systems... I think I spent an hour and a half trying to get my Mileage Plus account on United to work correctly with my daughter's phone and all this other stuff, partly because these systems are so complicated, but they're built in mainframes. A lot of the engineers, and this is going to sound morbid, but I think it's true, a lot of the engineers are dead. (00:19:58): They literally are passed away. They were written 10, 20 years ago and going in and touching that code is probably the last thing anyone wants to do, so nobody goes in there. It's all that side. Now, we can change that. I'm very excited about what it means to go in and improve things that people take for granted. That's a big one. That's a bit of an aside. I think that the other thing that I think is worth signaling is, I think that the way the skills that you need to be effective in today's world is an acceleration of what we were talking about last episode. We were talking about ICs, we were talking about hands-on, we're talking about opinion, even back then, before Claude and ChatGPT and others came out. (00:20:52): I think what we're now seeing is companies are looking very, very carefully at their staffing and they're asking themselves, one, do we need this many people? Did we overhire? Part of the reason is they're looking, "Hey, maybe we doubled our staff in the last five years." Lots of companies that are public have done that. "Did we get twice as much for them?" It was funny, when I was at Google, now over 10, 15 years ago, we used to ask ourselves, I was on an ancillary team. I wasn't in the search or the ads team. We used to ask ourselves, "How many people are really needed for Google to hit their numbers?" They were like, at that time, 20,000, 30,000, 40,000 people. If you ask someone who wasn't in tech, you're like, "Oh, probably 90% of those folks, obviously." (00:21:47): The answer's probably closer to 9%. Probably you need 500 people to keep the lights on and to build that business. You don't need 25,000, 30,000, 40,000 people. There's a huge amount of overhead where companies hire not just because they want to have bureaucrats, because they want to expand, they want to try new things. But I think that there's a judgment day that's come back where companies are like, "Look, we aren't getting as much for the staff that we grew in the last five years. This AI thing requires a totally different skillset." The combination is going to mean, this year I predict in the next 12 to 24 months, we're going to see massive shedding of staffs and then massive rehiring. But you might see a company shed 30,000 and hire 8,000, but the 8,000 people they're going to hire are going to all be AI first. (00:22:44): The 30,000 they're going to let go of are going to be in combination of, we didn't get as much for those folks that we needed and we want to set the destination differently with a much lighter payload, and that's dark. That's going to make this year and the next year going to be pretty, pretty challenging. I'll transition a little bit to my thoughts on people, but I'll pause for a second to see if this resonates with you.
turns.zh: 这仍然让我感到震惊。每个人都会说：“哦，最前沿的技术啊之类的。” 我觉得即便在今天，情况依然如此，但就在不久前，Cobalt（一种编程语言）的代码行数比其他任何语言都要多得多。大型机销售业务依然表现不俗，对IBM这样的公司来说，这是一个异常庞大的收入来源。部分原因在于这些系统……我记得自己花了一个半小时试图让女儿的手机与我的美联航Mileage Plus账户正常同步，部分原因是这些系统太复杂了，但它们都是用大型机开发的。很多工程师——这听起来可能有点残酷，但确实如此——很多工程师都已经去世了。（00:19:58）：他们真的已经不在人世了。这些代码是10年、20年前编写的，现在去修改这些代码可能是任何人最不愿意做的事，所以根本没人去动手。现在，我们可以改变这种局面。我对能改进人们认为理所当然的系统这件事感到非常兴奋。这很重要。这只是个小插曲。我认为还有一点值得关注的是，如今所需的技能与我们上期节目讨论的趋势是一致的。我们当时谈到了集成电路、动手能力、观点——甚至在Claude和ChatGPT等技术出现之前。（00:20:52）：我认为我们现在看到的是，公司正在非常仔细地审视员工配置，自我拷问：我们需要这么多人吗？我们招聘过度了吗？部分原因是他们会反思：“嘿，也许过去五年我们员工规模翻了一倍。” 很多上市公司都这么做了。“我们为这些员工付出了两倍的代价吗？” 这挺有趣的，我在谷歌工作的时候——那是10到15年前的事了——我们曾自问，我当时在一个辅助团队，不在搜索或广告团队。我们会问：“谷歌要达成目标，需要多少人？” 他们当时的数字是2万、3万、4万人。如果你问一个非技术人士，他会说：“哦，显然这些人里90%都是闲置的。” （00:21:47）：但实际答案可能更接近9%。你只需要500人就能维持运营，建立业务。不需要25000人、30000人、40000人。很多公司存在大量冗余，他们招聘不仅仅是为了增加官僚层级，而是为了扩张、尝试新事物。但我认为现在到了清算日，公司们开始反思：“看看，我们过去五年扩张的员工并没有带来足够的回报。AI这件事需要完全不同的技能组合。” 这种组合将意味着，在今年乃至未来12到24个月内，我们将看到大规模裁员和重新招聘。但你可能会看到某家公司裁掉3万人，招聘8000人，但这8000人将全部专注于AI。（00:22:44）：裁掉的3万人将包括两部分：一是这些员工的产出未达预期；二是我们想调整发展方向，采用更轻量级的配置。这很残酷。这将让今年和明年都变得极具挑战性。我会稍微谈谈对人才的看法，但先暂停一下，看看你们是否对此有共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's scary to hear. We're going to talk about what folks listening can do to do their best to be in that second bucket of being rehired and kept, because there's a lot you can do. There's a lot of people that know they need to change and adjust and they're not doing anything. Now we want to talk about maybe some of the blockers there. One thing I'll note is, I should have mentioned this earlier, I just did this report on the job market. Interestingly, as of today at least, we have the most open PM roles globally at tech companies in three plus years. The last time it was this high was during COVID, basically. There are some good news there at least for the PM role. I don't know.
turns.zh: 听到这个消息真是令人担忧。接下来我们要讨论的是，听众们可以如何努力争取进入被重新录用和留任的第二梯队，因为大家可以采取很多行动。很多职场人知道自己需要改变和调整，却始终无所作为。现在我们想探讨一下其中的阻碍因素。需要指出的是，我本该早些提及这一点——我刚完成了一份关于就业市场的报告。有趣的是，至少截至今天，全球科技公司中产品经理职位空缺数量创下三年多来新高。上一次达到如此高峰，还是在新冠疫情期间。至少对产品经理这个职位而言，这算是个好消息。但我也不确定具体情况。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Did that surprise you, Lenny?
turns.zh: 莱尼，你对此感到惊讶吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it did, because there's always this sense that, why do we need PMs? What's the point? We have AI to just built stuff, and like-
turns.zh: 是的，确实惊讶，因为总有人会问：我们为什么需要产品经理？有什么意义呢？反正有AI能直接开发产品啊，而且——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's the, why do we need PMs? What's the point? We have AI to just build stuff. And my sense, I've always been saying this, I feel like the PM skill is the most important, valuable skill of all the skills. And I know every role thinks this about their role. It's like, no, design. We design more than anything now. But I feel like what you said where it's the deciding what to build, deciding if this is good and great and ready and prioritizing, I feel like that's what remains. So to me, it makes sense.
turns.zh: 就是“为什么需要产品经理？有什么意义呢？”毕竟有AI能直接开发产品。而我的观点——我一直这么说——我觉得产品经理的技能是所有技能中最重要、最有价值的。我知道每个职位的人都觉得自己的工作最重要。比如设计师们总说自己设计工作最多。但我觉得产品经理最核心的职责在于决定要开发什么功能，判断一个功能是否优秀、是否成熟、是否值得优先推进。对我来说，这就是产品经理的价值所在。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: [inaudible 00:24:29] report came out in a fortuitous time because it was right before I was preparing to come on this show. And the three points I was going to make is builders are going to have the time in their lives. Comps actually up and the Bay Area is essentially back in favor. And I think those three things came very much loud and clear in your report. And I think the question around, hey, why are product managers doing so well? Why are there so many jobs? When in reality, a lot of product people that all of us know are struggling to find a role or we're hearing about these layoffs. I think it depends on how you define what a product manager is. And I think that for the first time, I think that we did have a dramatic shift in what's defined. We three years ago talked about, "Hey, product managers, there's lots of archetypes. Some archetypes are actually more in favor. This was the IC conversation, the builder conversation." (00:25:27): Now what we're essentially saying is the information mover is essentially going to become a dinosaur. And I think about half of the product people that grew into the industry have that skill and superpower. And then there were a set of people who got into product because they like to build stuff. And folks like yourself who were a founder who that was sort of the motivation into joining the industry, and then they found themselves into this thing called product management. Those folks are builders. And those people are the ones that are being hired by your survey. I think those product managers, everybody wants a builder. And I think that interestingly, lots of engineers are builders, lots of designers are builders, lots of marketing folks are builders. And I think Builders Wanted is going to be the big tagline for the next couple of years. (00:26:29): And it is so fun to build. I'll bet you, and this is a prediction, that if you had to choose between preparing a podcast and sitting in Codex or sitting in Claud Code and working on your laptop, you would prefer the latter.
turns.zh: 时机真是绝佳——这份报告发布的时机恰到好处，因为正值我准备参加本期节目的前夕。我原本要提的三点是：建筑商们将迎来人生中的黄金机遇，湾区房产估值实际回升，基本重获青睐。我认为报告中这三点观点清晰明了。关于“产品经理为何如此吃香？为何岗位需求如此旺盛？”这个问题，我认为关键在于如何定义产品经理的角色。三年前，我们曾讨论过“产品经理有多种类型，某些类型更受青睐”——这正是IC（信息传递者）与builder（构建者）之间的讨论。如今，我们可以断言：信息传递者将逐渐被淘汰。约半数入行者具备这种技能与超能力，而另一些人则因热爱构建而投身产品领域，还有像您这样的创始人，最初是受创业动机驱动，后来才发现自己转向了产品管理。这些人就是builder。您的调查结果也印证了这一点——市场青睐builder型产品经理。值得一提的是，许多工程师、设计师和市场人员都具备这种特质。“Builder Wanted”将成为未来几年的主旋律。（00:26:29）：构建的乐趣无穷。我敢打赌，如果让您在准备播客和坐在Codex或Claud Code上敲代码之间选择，您肯定会选择后者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It is so fun. Yeah. Just like progress. You just make so much [inaudible 00:26:49]. It's like, look at this thing go. It's getting better. It's just getting better.
turns.zh: 太有趣了。是啊，就像进步一样。你能感受到巨大的成就感[00:26:49]。看看这个项目进展得多顺利。它越来越完善了。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I mean, when I was a PM, I used to take a break and go change the light bulbs in the house. And the reason why I would change the light bulbs is that light bulb was broken, but then I replaced it and the light came on. And man, was that satisfying? Because in a product job, there is very few days of satisfaction because you don't really have the ability to see something broken that gets fixed. It's just part of the challenge in having responsibility without authority until now. Now you can participate in the joy. You can create a design. You don't have to wait for the designer and convince the designer to go and actually work through this or to put your stuff on a backlog. You don't have to do that. And so I think that the builders are going to have the time of their lives, and I think they're going to be very focused on judgment. (00:27:51): I think that they're going to invade other functions. I think there's going to be... When I started the group five years ago, we had, for the first two to three years, until we got to about 60, 70 people in this community of head of products, we had one founder. In the last 12 months, as we've gone to about 125, we have 14 founders. 14 people essentially have decided that their next job was not to take another product executive role, but to found. Founding CEO is now open to us. I have one person, very senior person in my group who interviewed for a CHRO position because they wanted a product manager background for the CHRO position.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，当我还是产品经理的时候，我会抽空去家里换灯泡。之所以要换灯泡，是因为灯泡坏了，但我换了之后，灯亮了。天哪，那种满足感太棒了！因为在产品工作中，很少有能亲眼见证问题被解决的满足感。直到现在，我都深有体会——在没有权力却要承担责任的情况下工作实在太难了。现在你可以参与到这种满足感中来了。你可以亲自设计产品，不用再等设计师来完成，也不用把需求塞进待办列表。这种感觉太棒了！所以我觉得产品建设者们将迎来黄金时代，他们会更加注重判断力。（00:27:51）我认为他们会跨越其他职能领域。五年前我组建这个社区时，最初两三年内，我们的产品负责人社区只有一位创始人。过去12个月里，我们扩展到约125人，现在有14位创始人。这些人决定不再担任产品高管职位，而是选择创业。如今，产品建设者们可以担任CEO一职了。我团队里有一位资深成员，曾面试过首席人力资源官职位，因为他们希望首席人力资源官能具备产品经理的背景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is CHRO?
turns.zh: 什么是CHRO？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: That's the chief HR person in the company. So you would never think that an HR person would be a former product manager, but now forward-leading companies are starting to say, "Hey, we need someone who can bring this obsolescence skill, this judgment skill, this empowerment skill, this builder skill to the function." In fact, the function might be easier to learn than the other parts of the job. And we're seeing that trend that product builders are going to have both a broader range of opportunities up and down the stack, and it won't be product managers, and engineers can become product leaders and product builders, and all of this blurring of the lines is going to take place. I think that unfortunately, the flip side has to be mentioned. I think that non-builders, and I think that anyone who sort of sees themselves as not loving, like sitting down and building something, and there may be reasons why, and we'll get into why you may not be in a position to find the time, let's say. (00:29:51): But if you're not a builder, if you're like, "Look, I'm not really into tech." People say this all the time, "Oh, I'm not really into tech." I just really found it to be a lucrative job. It's a role where my ability to communicate, my ability to move information, was where I ended up enjoying it. I love team building, those kinds of nerds, which by the way, I love all those things. But if you don't love building stuff, you're in trouble. And I mentioned about half the people are in that camp. So we're going to have that challenge where they're going to have to find, perhaps leave the tech industry. They might have to. It might be that they want to go build a new business outside of tech, but use some of these AI tools, or maybe they want to find a job completely foreign to tech. (00:30:45): But I think that this non-builder piece is sort of a mirror image of the builder growth story that we're seeing.
turns.zh: CHRO就是公司的首席人力资源官。所以你可能不会想到HR会出身于产品经理，但如今前沿的公司开始意识到，“嘿，我们需要能将产品经理的洞察力、判断力、赋权能力和建设能力引入到人力资源部门的人。” 事实上，相较于其他职能，人力资源部门可能更容易学习这些技能。我们看到，产品建设者们将获得上下游更广泛的机会，他们不再局限于产品经理，工程师也能晋升为产品领袖和产品建设者。所有这些职能边界的模糊将逐渐形成。遗憾的是，另一面也不得不提及。我认为非建设者，或者那些认为自己不喜欢坐下来构建东西的人——可能有各种原因，比如找不到时间——但如果你不热爱构建，你就陷入了困境。我提到大约一半的人属于这种情况。所以我们将面临挑战，他们可能不得不离开科技行业。他们或许想在科技领域之外创立新业务，利用一些AI工具，或者干脆寻找与科技完全无关的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many directions we can go here. One thing I want to throw out, it's kind of a hot take, and this came from a chat I just had with Amol, a Head of Growth at Anthropic. So he's Head of Growth, he's a PM and he had this really interesting point that as engineers can do so much more, PMs are getting squeezed because they have to stay on top of so many things, so many features, so many ideas, so much talk, so many things being said at them. And there's this push for PMs at companies to ship PRs, build stuff themselves. And what we took away from that chat is the leverage that PMs often have is a lot higher, not spending time coding and shipping, but instead just staying on top of all this stuff. And he's like, "We need more PMs now. There's so much for PMs to do because engineers are so fast." (00:31:41): So there's still need for prototyping to explore ideas and ideate and get feedback and align. But he had an interesting take that it's better I don't spend time shipping stuff. It's better I do higher leverage work as a PM.
turns.zh:
关于这个话题，我们可以从多个角度展开讨论。我想提一个有点激进的观点——这源于我刚和Anthropic的增长负责人Amol进行的一次聊天。作为增长负责人，Amol同时也是产品经理，他提出了一个很有趣的观点：随着工程师的能力不断提升，产品经理正面临着越来越大的挑战——他们需要同时处理太多的事情、太多功能、太多创意、太多的沟通和反馈。公司也越来越倾向于让产品经理直接参与代码开发和项目交付。我们从这次聊天中发现，其实产品经理的真正价值在于统筹协调各种事务，而非亲力亲为地写代码和交付成果。他甚至说：“现在我们更需要产品经理，因为工程师的效率太高了。”  (00:31:41):  
当然，原型设计、收集反馈和协调各方仍然是必要的。但他强调，产品经理不必专注于交付具体成果，而是应该把精力投入到更高价值的工作中。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: It depends what he means by shipping stuff because I think that if you have an engineering team of 50 people building things for your customers and you're like, "Hey, I want to be the 51st because that's how I get leveraged." I'm like, "Eh, it's kind of a cheap knockoff of an engineer." If on the other hand, the thing that you're building is ways to stay on top of what the 50 people are doing when in the past that was building tickets and backlogs and all of the things that we used to do to figure out organizations, manage standups, that's the information overload that's happening. (00:32:38): What we saw when the CPOs got together is all of the things they're building are ways to drive efficiency out of their product organizations. They're inside the building kind of development efforts. And I'm not sure that for the next five years, we'll continue to build software that way, but I think in the next two years, people are going to change the product operating system that they're working on. (00:33:04): And we're already seeing companies that stand up and they say, "Hey, we've fully automated the way we do product reviews. We've fully automated the way we do product standups." So to his point, look, if there's 15, 10 times the amount of stuff happening, we need judgment to determine whether it's good. These are good or bad changes. And right now, if it's manual, we're cooked. So it's a combination of hiring good product builders with judgment and then hiring increasingly folks whose entire job is to build the internal tools necessary to improve the decisioning, but it's not through hiring of humans and building management ethos, which is what it used to be in Zurp. It's actually through technology, but it's a totally different way of building software. And that's what gets people excited because they're like, "Wow, if I do this, I don't have to ever do a status report." I mean, that was a comment that was made. (00:34:01): I hate doing status reports. So now I just wrote something and my boss is happier because they get more detail. And that to me is incredibly exciting, but it is a different direction of what you're trying to deliver than something that goes out the door.
turns.zh:
这取决于他对“交付成果”的定义。我觉得如果一个50人的工程团队正在为客户开发产品，而你却想成为第51个成员，靠这种方式获取价值，那未免太不值了。另一方面，如果你开发的工具能帮助你实时掌握50人的动态——比如过去用于组织管理的工单系统、待办事项列表等——那才是真正在解决信息过载的问题。  
(00:32:38):  
在首席产品官们聚会时，我们发现他们打造的工具都是为了提升产品组织的效率，属于内部开发范畴。我不确定未来五年是否还会继续以这种方式开发软件，但未来两年内，人们必将重塑产品运营体系。  
(00:33:04):  
我们已经看到一些公司宣称：“我们完全自动化了产品评审流程，自动化了产品站会流程。”  Amol的观点很对：当待处理事务数量激增10倍、15倍时，我们需要判断哪些是有效的改进，哪些是无效的。目前靠人工管理已经不行了。所以，关键在于招聘善于判断的优秀产品经理，同时培养专注于开发内部工具的人才，以提升决策效率。这与Zurp时期的管理模式不同——过去靠的是人力和管理理念，而现在完全依赖技术。这是一种全新的软件开发思路，令人兴奋不已。比如有人说：“哇，如果我采用这种方法，就再也不用写状态报告了。”  (00:34:01):  
我讨厌写状态报告。所以现在我写了些东西，老板更满意了，因为能获取更多细节。这对我来说太棒了，但这与最终交付的产品完全是两个方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a good distinction and it makes all the sense. Basically, it's make yourself scale through software as much as possible. There's a big opportunity and it's fun. It's like you're building your own thing.
turns.zh: 这真是个绝妙的区分方式，完全说到点子上了。本质上，就是要尽可能通过软件实现自我升级。这是个巨大的机遇，也充满乐趣，就好像你在打造属于自己的事业。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: That's right. That's right. I think a few other things that I would just note around how things are going to change the next couple of years, I think that adults are still going to be needed. I think companies are going to grow, they're going to grow quickly. I think those that are driving some of these initiatives are classic founders and AI is great at supplementing a lot of things, but I think judgment comes in the form of a combination of expertise and wisdom. (00:34:54): And so I think that increasingly I hear from my groups that, "Hey, I'm attractive to this company because I have wisdom, but I stay hands-on. I have credibility with the founder so I can have a conversation with that individual in his or her language, but I have weight to my thinking. I have seen the movie. I have experience that actually would help them as they take this turn." So adults are still going to be important. (00:35:24): I think pace will continue to go up, partly because people will want to feed the beast, the sort of LLMs that are running at night. And I think partly because there's just such an opportunity to keep moving so much faster. And I think that's going to be dizzying and I'm not excited about what that causes for burnout. Sadly, I think that geography and actually diversity is going to take a step back. I think that we were very good about driving more breath. As we grew the industry, we started looking at people who were from different backgrounds to populate it, including different locations. But I think that because the AI wave is so heavily coming from the Bay Area, and because companies are hiring fewer folks, they're hiring people that look and act like themselves. So age, gender, I think, ethnic backgrounds, all of those are taking a hit. (00:36:28): And I think that we will have stepped back quite a number of years in the diversity of what we do. And so I worry, I mean, this is my personal worry, but I worry about that probably more now than I did in the last five years, because I think it's an underbelly of what we're seeing. And I don't think that anyone's intentionally doing anything, but I think when pace is so high, the fact is that women are having kids in those power years and they just don't have the time to allot to spending their nights and weekends in Claude Code. And so that's an impact. And we don't talk about it as an industry, but it's absolutely true. And then the last thing I would just say, and maybe this goes into some of the advice as well, is I think that one of the most surprising shifts we're seeing is your brands don't matter as much as how modern you are in your ability to deliver product. In the past, I think for the last 10 years, it's like, have you seen the movie before? And even in this last podcast episode we did, Lenny, we talked about, hey, brands matter, you really need to make sure.
turns.zh:
没错，没错。我想再补充几点关于未来几年行业变革的观察：首先，人才需求依然存在。企业会快速发展壮大，推动这些变革的核心人物往往是创始人。AI能在许多领域提供支持，但最终的判断仍需结合专业知识与智慧。（00:34:54）：我越来越多地从团队中听到这样的反馈：“我吸引了这家公司的注意，因为我有智慧，但我能亲力亲为。我与创始人建立了信任，能用对方熟悉的语言交流，又能为决策提供有力支撑。我看过大局，拥有实战经验，能助力他们转型。” 所以，成熟人才仍具重要价值。
（00:35:24）：发展速度会持续加快，一方面是因为人们急于喂养夜间运行的LLM模型；另一方面则源于抓住机遇的冲动。但这种高速发展可能带来职业倦怠风险。令人担忧的是，地域多样性与包容性或将倒退。我们曾积极推动行业多元化，吸纳不同背景、不同地域的人才。但随着AI浪潮主要源自湾区，企业招聘时更倾向于招募与自己相似的人才——年龄、性别、种族背景等多样性都在退步。
（00:36:28）：行业多元性或将倒退数年。我个人对此愈发担忧，因为这已成为行业隐性问题。虽然无人刻意歧视，但高强度的工作节奏导致女性在事业黄金期生育，难以抽出时间进行周末学习。这是不可忽视的现实。
最后，我想说，最令人惊讶的转变之一是：品牌影响力已让位于产品交付能力。过去10年，人们常问“你看过相关电影吗？”在最新播客中，我们探讨了品牌的重要性，但现实是，现代化的产品交付能力才是核心竞争力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like personal brands?
turns.zh: 比如个人品牌？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, personal brands. "Hey, I've worked for this company, they've delivered products, they've been at scale." So then people are like, "Oh, that person certainly knows what [inaudible 00:37:54] doing." And it's like, "Well, tell me about all the different experiences you've had." But now if every way of building software and how we deliver product is completely alien to how it was in the last 10 years, how you delivered in that sort of version one is going to be less and less relevant. So lots and lots of feedback that I'm hearing from interviews is, put you in a scenario. What tools do you use? What's your judgment? How do you think? It's not about five years ago, you shipped this thing, what was your thinking that went into it? And so how modern you are now becomes the career advice, not did you pick up the established brands? (00:38:42): Because what if the established brands is very much working in a way that's not current? You work there for six years, you come out, and it feels like you're in a totally different world. So that's why I think the next two years and these changes are so profound, and quite frankly confusing to people.
turns.zh: 是的，个人品牌。“嘿，我曾在这家公司工作，开发过产品，业务规模也做起来了。” 然后人们会说：“哦，那个人肯定很懂行。”但接着就会被问：“能给我讲讲你所有不同的经历吗？”然而，如果你现在构建软件和交付产品的所有方式与过去10年的做法完全不同，那么你在1.0版本中积累的经验就越来越不适用了。所以我在面试中听到的大量反馈都是：设定一个场景，你用了哪些工具？你的判断力如何？你怎么看待问题？而不是五年前你交付了某个项目时的思考过程。（00:38:42）：如今你所具备的现代技能正成为职业建议的核心，而非追随已有的品牌路线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such an interesting insight that the logo, it used to be fancy to have all these logos on your resume, and now you're saying sometimes that may hurt you because that company's not seen as a very AI forward company. And second of all, people are looking for just like, "What have you actually done? Are you actually aware what's going on?"
turns.zh: 这真是个有趣的见解——曾经简历上堆满各种Logo会显得很高大上，而现在人们却认为这可能反而会拖后腿，因为这些公司被视为不重视AI的落后者。其次，大家更关注的是：“你实际做了什么？你对当前趋势有何洞察？”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Well, I was just going to say, some of those biggest brands, it's hard to even talk about what you've done. It's like, if you're working at Meta and you spent two years and I managed to make this piece of this algorithm go a little faster, and by the way, it had a huge impact. And frankly, it was incredibly hard to navigate the hallways, and to make that decision and to find incrementality. I mean, as someone who has worked there, I understand and respect that, and that is a promotable achievement, but it just falls very flat on a conversation where someone's living in the future and product is now totally different. So that distinction is the thing that I want to just call out that, "Hey, that's happening every day right now."
turns.zh: 嗯，我想说的是，一些大品牌的项目，你甚至很难解释清楚自己的贡献。比如在Meta工作两年，成功让某个算法运行得更快，虽然这确实带来了重大影响，但要在复杂的组织中找到增量改进实在太难了。作为在那里工作过的人，我理解并尊重这种成就，但在一个以未来为导向、产品形态已然彻底变革的环境中，这种成就很难产生共鸣。因此，我想强调的是，“这种变化每天都在发生。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what you're saying there, which is a really powerful point, is that the skills that used to be really valued in product managers are changing pretty substantially.
turns.zh: 所以你提出的观点非常有力，那就是产品经理曾经备受推崇的技能正在发生巨大变革。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. And in fact, maybe almost looked upside down in terms of importance. In some ways, we start our careers as builders, many of us, and then we get taught that leverage, scale, organizing, streamline, empowering, enabling. Don't do the build yourself, get others to do it, stop working on the car work on the factory. That is the maturation of our industry. And then you find out that, well, what if it turns out the scale can be done very differently and all we care about is your opinion and what you build. That's very jarring and that's what we're living through right now.
turns.zh: 是的。事实上，这些技能的重要性可能已经完全颠倒过来了。在某种程度上，我们很多人都是从构建者起步，后来被教导要善于利用杠杆、规模化组织、精简流程、赋能他人。不要亲力亲为，而是让别人去干活，从修车到管理工厂。这是我们行业的成熟历程。然而现在我们发现，原来的规模化路径可能行不通了，人们只关注你的洞察力和实际成果。这确实令人震惊，而这正是我们当下所处的时代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's follow this thread of specific advice to PMs right now, whether they're mid-career, senior, getting started. What are some specific things that you think people should do to do well in this emerging future?
turns.zh: 那么，针对当前处于职业生涯中期、资深或刚刚起步的产品经理，具体有哪些建议呢？你认为人们应该做些什么才能在新兴的未来中脱颖而出？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Change is really hard for us. And I think as humans, we're not really designed to change very easily. If you think about it, I was thinking about why is it hard for us to change when in some ways change can lead us to much better outcomes. We're almost told to change less as we grow older. When you're a kid, you fall down a ton. But Lenny, when was the last time you fell down?
turns.zh: 改变对我们来说确实很难。我觉得作为人类，我们的生理构造并不适合轻易改变。仔细想想，当改变有时能带来更好的结果时，为何我们却如此抗拒？随着年龄增长，人们似乎被告知要尽量减少改变。小时候，我们经常摔倒。但莱尼，你上次摔倒是什么时候？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not often, except my son loves to pretend like we're falling, so there's a lot of pretend fall.
turns.zh: 不常摔倒，不过我儿子特别喜欢假装我们在摔倒，所以他经常这样表演。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And when you pretend fall, it's probably pretty jarring. It's probably relatively new.
turns.zh: 而当你假装摔倒时，那种冲击感可能很强烈。这对他来说可能还是新鲜体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. For him, it's so fun. He loves it, but yeah, for me, I'm like oh, my God, such a long ways down.
turns.zh: 是啊。对他来说很有趣，他特别喜欢这样。但对我来说，每次都感觉天哪，摔下去可真够吓人的。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: it's no fun, right? Yeah. And I think that it's funny because you watch kids and it's normal for them to reinvent everything they do. "Oh, I'm learning to crawl. Oh, now this walking thing, crawling, that's not for me." It's why kids learn languages so quickly because they are not afraid to make mistakes and they go through things much more rapidly. It's why you teach your kids to learn how to ski early because boy, I've just made a decision. Hey, I've never been a skier and I'm just too old to do it. "I think that we are trained to find a happy medium and then make as few changes as possible, find a partner, get settled down, find a job, try to stay. It's a failure to transition to a new job if you can avoid it. That's our entire model. And so we create also, in some ways, a mental block around this idea of reinventing oneself. (00:42:53): When you are told to reinvent, to when you are told to change, your first thing you think about is it really necessary? Boy, it seems exhausting. I worked so hard to get here. Why would I need to? And I think in the most inner psyche of some of us, its, that just wasn't the deal. The deal was I did what I was supposed to, went to school, I worked hard, I got a job, I built the brand, I got to be a manager, I'm making the income, I have the whatever it might be, the partner, the family, all this stuff. But in the back of your mind, it's like, "I just don't know why. Why did we get here? I don't want to do it. I want to go back to the world where I can just keep doing things." 我觉得我们应该去找你所描述的那个人。现在有个人坐在那里，非常害怕，他是一名产品经理，他会说：“天哪，我的工作，变化太快了，我很紧张，我得想清楚我的职业生涯该怎么走。” 但我通常会问他一个问题：“你真的热爱你的工作吗？”如果你把参加过的会议用绿色、黄色和红色标注，然后持续一周观察颜色分布，我敢打赌，大多数产品组织中的项目经理，他们的图表上显示的都是黄色和红色。而我告诉你，那些真正转入构建模式的人，他们的图表上大多是绿色和黄色。然而，他们中的大多数人却坐着，感到非常害怕，觉得自己被困住了。所以我的建议是，如何在心理和行动上从恐惧和观望的状态转变为投入行动的状态？（00:55:01）：我注意到一点，这让我很惊讶，就是当他们第一次使用新工具时会体验到快乐。每个人都有自己的故事，而且各不相同，但都非常个人化。比如，“哦，我之前是用那种方法做事的，然后突然间我建成了这个东西。” 很多时候，他们会说：“我和我的搭档用我开发的这个应用程序”，或者“我开发了一个用于追踪收件箱的参谋长应用程序”，或者“我现在用这个东西来控制家里的灯光”之类的小玩意儿。通常还伴随着一个故事，比如“我整晚没睡”，或者“我花了很多时间和朋友聊天或不断改进”，或者“我刚刚和Claude聊了这个”。甚至我的妻子也有故事，她正在考虑创业，从使用AI做商业计划到实际进行市场测试。（00:56:09）：每个人都有这样的快乐时刻，然后就上瘾了。就像中了毒一样。在那一刻，他们跨越了从恐惧到快乐的门槛，而快乐是消除职业倦怠的最佳良药，也是创造机会的关键。因为当你感到快乐时，工作就不再是工作了。如果不去构建，产品管理对大多数人来说就是工作。而我们现在正进入一个产品管理将以快乐而非工作为核心的时代。所以你只需要找到一条通往快乐的路。一旦你找到了，你的心理就会创造出时间，不再觉得自己让别人失望，还能积蓄能量，因为人们的能量远超他们的想象。他们只是被定义为产品管理的单调性所累。所以最重要的建议是：你找到快乐了吗？（00:57:10）：现在有一种人会说：“这一切都不快乐。我觉得整个事情很无聊，甚至令人作呕。我真的不喜欢它。” 我会说：“好吧，那你可能不适合我们行业的下一个版本了。” 你应该尊重这一点，也要诚实面对自己。但现在有很多产品从业者非常焦虑，一旦他们跨越了鸿沟，他们就会变得更快乐。他们只需要找到创造快乐时刻的方法，无论是个人应用还是工作中的其他应用。如果你是听众中的领导者，你应该在你的团队中寻找这些快乐时刻，因为这具有感染力，让人们兴奋不已。这就是我喜欢做这份工作的原因，我喜欢构建东西，我也迷上了它，并且一直全情投入。我还试图找到能让我代入编码状态的电视节目。
与此同时，我想看电视，但又想同时专心编程[听不清00:58:07]。

turns.zh: 说到这儿。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: They're built on books. These books are like, they're structured and all that. So Alex Cross or Jack Ryan. You know what's hilarious is... And when you get older, you remember shows that you love, but you don't remember the plot. So one time I just binge watch a season of 24, the show that I loved back in the day. But frankly, I watched it and I kind of knew what was going on, but I vibe coded the whole time because it was like, "Hey, I'm paying attention here, but I'm staying engaged."
turns.zh: 这些剧集大多改编自原著小说。原著本身结构严密，情节连贯。比如《亚历克斯·克罗斯》系列和《杰克·瑞安》系列。最有趣的是……等你年纪大了，回想起自己喜欢的剧集时，往往记不清具体情节了。有次我一口气看完了整季《24小时》——这部我年轻时超爱的剧集。但说实话，我虽然看完了剧情，但全程都在用这种“保持专注”的方法看剧，心里想：“嘿，我在认真看，但还是得保持专注。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
