turns.zh: 等等，咱们接着聊。你用的AI开发栈是什么？你用什么工具开发项目？有没有自己开发的项目，又有哪些是用“vibe coding”完成的？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I kind of am pretty all in on Claude these last three months. I was, for a month, pretty aggressive on Codex because I found some of their newer stuff to be, especially with the highest level of reasoning to be quite advanced. I find it hard to switch between tools I try to standardize to be direct. Look, the things that I build, I build a bunch of web properties for my community. So anytime I see something that I can obsolete and code, I try to build code around it. So if you had 100 people, one natural thing you want people to do is to meet each other and 100 people can't meet 99 other [inaudible 00:59:42]. So you have to be thoughtful around who's the best person to meet and how do you match people up? How do you make sure that you match people with people they haven't met before? What are their haves or their wants? (00:59:54): That entire thing used to be me sitting down and thinking like, "Oh, Jay-Z would really appreciate meeting Annie, but I don't know if they've met before." Now I write software to do that. I write an agent that goes in and actually does matching. I write an agent to figure out, "Hey, what are all the jobs that my head of products are hiring? How do we make sure that we make those available, but then build a mailing list of folks who I think when they're interested in work can get matched up automatically." So the next generation of recruiting. I think a lot about using AI for content. So when I sit down, I have an AI that takes questions from people and then it's trained on my content and it gives answers. But then I read those questions, evaluate the answers, and I'm like, "Hey, this is a theme I'm hearing." And then I sit down and I write down, when do the LLMs and I disagree, I go through. (01:00:52): And so all of these things or anything that I'm doing that I think I can replicate, I try to obsolete myself. When I started my first job, I asked the best engineer that I worked with, who still is one of the best engineers I've ever met, "What's the definition of a great engineer?" And I thought it would be like, "Oh, someone who's got this degree or is well versed in this technology stack." He's like, "Well, the best engineer I know is my dad." And of course, this was before tech in that case. And he's like, "And my dad's definition is still my favorite, which is an engineer is someone who obsoletes themselves from everything they do. That's the definition of a great engineer." And I've taken that to every job that I've worked at. (01:01:43): And it's funny because you'll run into people that are like, "Oh no, no, I don't want to obsolete myself. That's my job." And I was like, "Ah, I think if obsolete there'll be a better job for me." What AI has done that has basically put an [inaudible 01:01:57] on that. If you can obsolete by just asking the AIs to do this for you. So why I'm saying that is my stack is what can I do to obsolete anything and everything I do on a daily basis?
turns.zh: 过去三个月，我对Claude可谓是全情投入。我曾在Codex上非常积极地参与讨论，因为我发现他们的一些最新成果，尤其是最高水平的推理技术，实在是太前沿了。我发现自己很难在试图标准化的工具之间切换，以保持直观易用。比如，我为社区搭建了许多网络平台。所以每当我发现有可以被代码替代的功能时，我都会着手开发相关代码。再比如，假设有100个人，你肯定希望他们能相互认识，但99个人无法相互结识（00:59:42）。所以你得仔细考虑谁是最合适的匹配对象，以及如何有效配对。比如，他们各自的资源或需求是什么？（00:59:54）过去我得自己坐下来思考：“哦，Jay-Z肯定很想认识Annie，但我不知道他们是否见过面。” 现在我写软件来实现这一功能。我开发了一个匹配算法，可以自动配对。我还开发了一个代理程序，用于整理产品负责人正在招聘的职位信息，确保这些职位信息公开，同时建立一个邮件列表，方便感兴趣的人自动匹配。这就是下一代招聘模式。我还深入思考如何利用AI处理内容。比如，当有人提问时，我让AI根据我的内容进行回复，然后我评估这些答案，发现其中有共通的主题。接着我会坐下来写下心得，当LLM和我存在分歧时，我会逐一核对。（01:00:52）所以，任何我认为可以被替代的任务，我都会努力自我淘汰。刚开始工作时，我问当时共事的最优秀的工程师（至今仍是我遇到过的最出色的工程师之一）：“怎样才算优秀的工程师？”我以为答案会是“拥有某个学位或精通某个技术栈的人”。他却说：“我认识的最优秀的工程师是我的父亲。”当然，那时他还没进入科技行业。他说：“我父亲的定义至今仍是我的最爱——优秀的工程师就是能自我淘汰一切的人。” 我将这条准则应用到每一份工作中。（01:01:43）有趣的是，你会遇到一些人说：“不不，我不想淘汰自己，那是我的工作。”我回应道：“但淘汰自己才能找到更好的工作机会。” 而AI的出现恰好为这一理念提供了支持——你只需让AI替你完成淘汰任务。所以我现在强调的核心是，如何淘汰日常工作中的所有重复环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. I love hearing these stories. What I find as the best tactic here is just solve your own problem. Think about something that's not great in your day-to-day or something you just want to improve and just like... And it sounds so easy. All you do is go to, I don't know, Lovable or install Claude Code, download Codex and just tell it. I want to build a dashboard to control my Sonos and then it just tells you, walks you through everything you need to explore. And so that's a pretty advanced thing to try, but it's just like English. It sounds like I have no know-how to do this. You just tell it. Here's what I want to do, just like a person and it helps you figure it out.
turns.zh: 太酷了。我喜欢听这些故事。我觉得这里最有效的策略就是解决自己的问题。想想你日常生活中不顺心的事，或者你想改进的地方，然后就……听起来很简单。只要去Lovable或者安装Claude Code，下载Codex，然后告诉它：“我想建一个控制Sonos的仪表板。”它就会一步步指导你完成所有操作。这听起来挺高级的，但其实很简单。就像说英语一样。听起来好像我没这本事似的。但你只要告诉它：“我想做这个。”就像和人交流一样，它就能帮你解决问题。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Well, and I agree with you. And then I think the question is what skill do you have to have? For a while I was like, "Oh, that's a systems engineering skill because you need to be able to train the AIs to go after things." But I'm watching my wife and how she works, and she's not an engineer by any means, and she's getting tons of value. You don't even need to be an engineer. You just have to be opinionated on what you want to see.
turns.zh: 我完全同意你的看法。关键问题在于你需要具备什么技能？之前我觉得这得是系统工程师的技能，因为你得训练AI去处理各种任务。但我观察我妻子的工作方式，她根本不是工程师，却能从中获得巨大价值。你甚至不需要是工程师，只要对自己想要的东西有清晰的认知就行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And know what you want. Yeah, know what good looks like.
turns.zh: 然后当你实现目标时，那种顿悟的感觉就来了。之前可能一直卡在某个环节，现在突然豁然开朗。接着你坐下来，开始思考：“嘿，我以前得亲自做这些事，现在我的智能助手帮我搞定了。接下来我还能让助手做些什么，让生活更轻松呢？” 这时候你就抓住了窍门。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And then the moment that you get it, it's when the light bulb turns on when it wasn't working before. And now you sit down and there's this moment where it's like, "Hey, I used to have to go and work to do this, but now my agent's doing this. And then what's the next agent I could do to make my life a little bit better?" And that's where you catch the bug.
turns.zh: 产品经理（或者任何职位）都能让工作变得更有乐趣，这真是令人惊叹。但我们今天主要讲产品经理。就比如你看看自己每天的幸福感曲线图，未来完全可以变得更快乐。我觉得人们很难意识到这一点，他们总觉得：“哇，真的吗？我能更热爱这份工作？我从没想过。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a powerful thought that your job can be much more joyful as a product manager, as any function, but we're focusing on PMs. Just like if you look at your pie chart today of how happy you are during the day, you can actually be much happier in this future. And I think that's hard for people to really think, just realize, "Oh, wow, okay. I can actually love this job so much more? I did not imagine that."
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这是因为你一直盯着变化。变化就像警钟一样刺耳。我们很难听到变化的声音，因为变化太可怕了。我很理解这种心理。所以我觉得听众如果能理解这一点就好了：未来会有更好的世界，但你必须穿过那条隧道。隧道很痛苦，可能意味着你得换工作。我的预测是，未来五年，绝大多数听众都会换工作，或者因为公司无法保持现代化而被淘汰。公司必须保持现代化，否则就会裁员。所以因为变化显而易见，人们对强加给他们的变化心存戒备。这是人之常情。但我和人们交流时，会抛开过去的成败，专注于如何从中创造价值。最好的结果已经足够美好了。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. And I think that it's because you're staring at change. And I think change is such an alarm bell. It's hard to hear the voice that says the thing that you are changing or the things you don't love because change is so hard for us that it's so scary. And I respect that. So I think that if your listeners are able to sort of understand that, hey, there is a world which is better, but I have to go through the tunnel and the tunnel sucks. And the tunnel may mean that I'm going to have to change jobs. My prediction is the vast majority of people that are listening to this will be in a different job in the next five years because they will either choose to move to something because that company will struggle to stay modern just like we're describing. People need to stay modern, companies need to stay modern, or their companies are going to be shedding and returning off staff. And so because change is apparent, I think it's just so deafening that people are very much gun shy to be excited about something that's forced on them. And let's be honest, it's been forced on everyone and it's not something that they chose. So that's why I have a lot of empathy. But when I talk to people, I try to dig through, forget what's happened and why. How do we make the best out of it? And the best is pretty good.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这就是因为你一直在面对变化。变化就像警钟一样刺耳。我们很难听到变化的声音，因为变化太可怕了。我很理解这种心理。所以我觉得听众如果能理解这一点就好了：未来会有更好的世界，但你必须穿过那条隧道。隧道很痛苦，可能意味着你得换工作。我的预测是，未来五年，绝大多数听众都会换工作，或者因为公司无法保持现代化而被淘汰。公司必须保持现代化，否则就会裁员。所以因为变化显而易见，人们对强加给他们的变化心存戒备。这是人之常情。但我和人们交流时，会抛开过去的成败，专注于如何从中创造价值。最好的结果已经足够美好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So say we've convinced a listener, "Okay, I need to make a change. I need to lean into this. I need to take this seriously. I can't just sit back and hope it all works out okay." And then they maybe found a moment of joy. They built something that's super cool and just like, "Hey, check this out." What other advice do you have for folks listening to help them be to survive... I don't know, let's not say survive, but just thrive in this future that is emerging for product people.
turns.zh: 假设我们成功说服了一位听众：“好吧，我需要做出改变。我得全力以赴。我不能只是坐等一切顺利。” 然后他们或许找到了片刻的喜悦。他们打造出某个超酷的东西，然后兴奋地说：“嘿，看看这个。” 对于听众们，您还有什么建议能帮助他们在未来这个新兴的职场环境中生存下来……嗯，也许不该说‘生存’，而是‘蓬勃发展’。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, I like thrive. I definitely think that you find that moment of joy, you have the engineering mindset, which is, "Hey, I want to obsolete myself on something that I do today." Again, reduce the less joyful parts of my job is a good starting point. I think that you have to find ability to increase pace. The next two years requires a lot of fire in the belly, a lot of agency that I know everyone talks about. So for example, if you were to leave a job and start a new job, you probably don't view the new job year one at the same pace that you viewed year five in your last job. You need to kind of bring it. If you have a new relationship and if you've come off of a long-term relationship, my suspicion is your first year of that relationship, you put your best foot on. (01:06:47): This is what I'm asking. You got to find that reserve. You've got to make time. You've got to maybe disappoint others in a way that you haven't in the past in order to create time for you to stay current, find that joy, obsolete yourself from the things that are not worth it. I think the other thing you have to do is you have to swallow your ego. I don't want a single person saying, "Hey, I was a X, Y, Z leader. I would only consider roles at that same level." I want people, this is an extension of our last conversation, is not only is it in vogue to be hands-on and I see it's kind of a necessity, I need everyone to sort of say, "Look, if everything's changing, it doesn't matter what we've done the past. That brand doesn't matter as we discussed." You have to have an egoless perspective of how to stay current. (01:07:40): And you would be not only willing, but actually look for ways to even take something smaller in order to make sure that you're kind of going through the tunnel correctly. And then ultimately, part of the way we swallow that ego is you stay long-term focused. You say, "Look, if the way we build product is changing so aggressively, my job is to spend the next couple of years being on the boat that's leaving the station and going to the new world. Once I get to the new world, the cream rises to the top, I'll take my skills, my leadership, and I'll go through it. But in the next few years, if everything's changing, I definitely want to be current." And that means you have to have a long-term focus. (01:08:26): My property is called the skip, of the community and everything. They all kind of come down to this word called the skip. And I chose that word because the best career advice is always not thinking about the next move, but the move after. What's the skip job? What's the skip opportunity? Well, in this world, it's not about what's an opportunity now and what's the journey. It's about making sure that your skip opportunity is saved and you are able to get that high salary, you're able to get one of those premier builder jobs, and that's the world that you have to have and the mindset you have to have.
turns.zh: 是的，我更倾向于‘蓬勃发展’。我坚信，你要找到那一刻的喜悦，拥有工程师思维——‘嘿，我想用今天的技能去淘汰自己’。减少工作中不那么令人愉悦的部分，是个不错的起点。我认为你必须找到提升节奏的能力。未来两年需要满腔热忱和积极主动的精神。比如，如果你跳槽到新公司，可能不会像看待老公司第五年时那样看待第一年。必须全力以赴。如果你开始新恋情，而刚结束一段长期关系，我猜你会全力以赴地投入第一年。（01:06:47）这就是我想问的——你得储备能量。你得腾出时间。可能需要以一种过去未曾有过的方式让别人失望，从而为自己留出保持敏锐的时间，找到那份喜悦，淘汰掉那些不值得投入的工作。另一个要点是放下自负。我不希望任何人说：“嘿，我曾是X、Y、Z级别的领导，我只考虑同级别的职位。”我想说（延续我们上次的讨论），亲力亲为不仅是潮流，更是生存必需。每个人都得意识到：既然一切都在变革，过去的成就已不再重要。必须以无私的视角保持敏锐。（01:07:40）你不仅要愿意，甚至要主动寻找更小的机会，确保自己能顺利过渡。最终，放下自负的关键在于保持长期视野。你要说：“既然产品开发方式变化如此剧烈，接下来几年我的任务就是搭上即将启程的列车，驶向新世界。一旦抵达新世界，优秀者必将脱颖而出，我会带上技能和领导力，继续前行。但未来几年，一切都在变革，我必须紧跟时代。”这意味着你必须具备长远的眼光。（01:08:26）我的社区叫‘Skip’，一切都归结于‘Skip’这个词。我选择这个词，是因为最棒的职业建议永远不是考虑下一步，而是下下一步。什么是‘Skip’工作？什么是‘Skip’机会？在这个世界里，关键不在于当下有什么机会，旅程如何，而在于确保你的‘Skip’机会得以保留，让你能拿高薪，获得那些顶级建设者的职位。这才是你必须具备的思维和心态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something you mentioned earlier was really interesting that in the next five years, you predict that most people's jobs will be very different. What are you imagining there? Will there still be this product manager role? Will PMs need to move closer to engineering? What's the Venn diagrams or spectrum you're seeing of where current PMs may go?
turns.zh: 你之前提到的一个观点非常有趣——你预测未来五年大多数人的工作岗位将发生巨大变化。你具体想象的是怎样的情景？产品经理这个角色还会存在吗？产品经理是否需要更贴近工程部门？你所设想的当前产品经理可能转向的领域的维恩图或光谱图是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, I definitely think that there's a world where PMs go to every industry as what I would call the agents of change because the PMs are the ones that can talk. They're the ones that have the broadest view of the organization, but they look at it through the technical lens. And my hope is that most of our PMs are the first to the tools, and hence they're the change agents within their company. So let's just play this out. In the next year, we start to see all these product organizations changing the way they build product. And all of a sudden, the way we build product is gentrified and really, really thoughtful and really far along. (01:10:09): And then 12 months later, the marketing, the sales organization, the HVAC company that was bought by the private equity firm, the school down the road, everything's like, "Boy, we're not current. We're going to get obsolete. Who do we bring in to be in charge of this change? Well, this person works in the future. We need to get to future." So I'm really bullish that product leaders are going to be like those dandelion, whatever you call it, seeds when you blow it and they just go everywhere. I have that vision. Meanwhile, I think a lot of people going into product might be coming from design, might be coming from data science, might be coming from engineering. Because the ones that have judgment, the ones that can talk, the ones that want to stay current, they might be like, "Well, I don't necessarily want to just stay in my lane. I have a point of view as to how this should work." (01:11:10): As you said, from a designer point of view, designers may have a lot of those skills and opinions on what it should look like. Maybe their platform won't be the pixels or the visuals, they will be the product itself and they can adjacently move into product. So I think you're going to see this crazy influx and then this amazing kind of exodus. And then you'll also see folks that are like, "Ooh, I don't know if I can get in." So I know that's a confusing kind of set of three changes, but that explains why so many people have anxieties. All three of these are happening instantaneously.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实认为产品经理有可能进入每个行业——我称他们为变革的推动者，因为产品经理善于沟通。他们对组织有着最宏观的视野，但却以技术视角看待事物。我希望我们的大多数产品经理能率先掌握新工具，从而成为所在公司的变革先锋。让我们设想一下未来一年：我们开始看到所有产品团队都在改变产品开发方式。突然间，产品开发方式变得更先进、更具前瞻性且更加精细化。（01:10:09）12个月后，营销部门、销售团队、被私募基金收购的暖通公司、附近的学校等各界人士都会感叹：“天啊，我们落伍了。我们要被淘汰了。该找谁来主导这场变革呢？嗯，这个未来的人才正好能胜任。”因此，我坚信产品领袖将像蒲公英种子一样四处播撒。我有这样的愿景。与此同时，我认为许多进入产品领域的人可能来自设计、数据科学或工程领域。因为那些善于判断、善于沟通、渴望紧跟潮流的人可能会说：“嗯，我不一定要局限于自己的专业领域。我对产品应该如何运作有自己的见解。”（01:11:10）正如你所说，从设计师的角度来看，设计师可能拥有许多这样的技能和见解。也许他们的平台不再是像素或视觉效果，而是产品本身，并且他们可以顺势进入产品领域。因此，我认为我们将看到疯狂的人才涌入和惊人的人才流失。然后你还会看到有人说：“哦，我不确定自己能否进入这个领域。” 我知道这三个变化的组合令人困惑，但这也解释了为什么这么多人感到焦虑。这三个变化都将瞬间发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a line. They thought they buried us. They didn't know that we were seeds that I think about.
turns.zh: 有一句话：他们以为埋葬了我们，却不知道我们是种子。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I love that. We're into a lot of the darker...
turns.zh: 我喜欢这点。我们讨论了很多更黑暗的方面……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, there's this hilarious tweet that just came out the other day that I have here-
turns.zh: 说到这儿，前几天刚有条搞笑的推文，我这儿有——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this hilarious tweet that just came out the other day that I have here, where this guy describes the only four jobs that will remain in the future. So the only four jobs that exist in the future: one is product engineer vibe-code or PM slop-cannon. Number two is security SRE infra person. Number three is hot people, which is getting people to buy your stuff, customer service. (01:12:28): Remember, there are many ways to be... oh no, here's how they put it: "Present a easy UX to the world" is that category. And then grownups, which is your point of just like adults. Yeah. (01:12:38): So I think there's some truth to this.
turns.zh:
最近有条超级搞笑的推文刚火起来，我这儿有截图。这人列举了未来仅存的四种工作岗位。第一种是产品工程师、写代码的，或者产品经理、拍马屁的。第二种是安全、运维、基础设施人员。第三种是"搞定事儿的"，也就是负责销售、客服的。（01:12:28）：记住，成功人士有很多种定义……哦不，他们是这么说的："为用户提供简洁易用的体验"，这就属于这一类。然后是"成熟人士"，简而言之就是做事靠谱的成年人。是啊。
（01:12:38）：我觉得这说法挺有道理的。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I read that and I agree with that. I mean, I think the adults exist and I think anyone that's the top of their field that can talk and that essentially is opinionated and can go broad, that's kind of the third point of hot people.
turns.zh: 我读了这段话，深有同感。我的意思是，成熟人士确实存在。那些行业顶尖、能言善道、见解独到、思维开阔的人，就是"搞定事儿的"这类人的典型代表。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that's actually... that reminds me. So Amol, the head of growth at Anthropic, made this really interesting point that so much of his time now, more and more, is alignment as a product manager. And we were joking, what's the harder alignment problem, aligning people in a company or AI's AGI? (01:13:07): And it feels like that's a remaining... and it's part of what you described, somebody that can get shit done, a change agent. And a big part of that is what a PM often is doing a lot of their time, is creating alignment internally around what we will be doing, what we're prioritizing, that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 这让我想起Anthropic的增长负责人Amol提到的一个有趣观点。他说，现在作为产品经理，越来越多时间要花在协调各方意见上。我们当时开玩笑说，协调公司内部人员和协调人工智能（AGI）哪个更难？（01:13:07）：感觉这还是个悬而未决的问题……这也和你提到的类似，既要能把事情办成，又要充当变革推动者。PM们大部分时间都在做的，就是围绕团队目标、优先事项等达成共识。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. And I think that if you dissect what alignment looks like, a lot of alignment was getting people the right information, the ground-level truth. That problem is dramatically better. And that part of the job, frankly, just absolutely sucked. Whether it was the status report or... I was on projects where there was docs that were sent to me, and then I would change the doc to then send it to my boss, and then that boss would send it to... and it was just this movement of information where the ground truth was buried in some part of the organization, and then there were all these people that were putting on their spin. (01:14:05): That, I think, is changing. But to your point, now someone has to decide, and someone has to have an opinion on what to fight for. And that conversation is now much clearer to have. Because you know the ground truth, there's less spin. The CEO can literally ask their agent, "Well, what is the situation? How is this performing? What does this customer really want? How does this affect the system? Is this really something that we want to change the product to enable?" (01:14:33): So that conversation can happen, but now people can fight it out with real credence. And if you're a product person that really does have an opinion and wants to make a point, you have a forum. So alignment won't go away. It's not going to have as much theatrics. And I think a lot of companies that are larger do have theatrics that I think AIs are going to remove. (01:14:59): And I don't know of many PMs, there's some that lived for the theatrics, but frankly, most of them were like, "This just seems like a fricking waste of time." I mean, it's so telling that 80%, I bet you, this is a statement, 80%, if you truly ask your PM, "Do you really want that boss's boss job, or do you want their day? Not the pay, not the credibility, not the stature, but do you want their back-to-back meetings?" I bet you most of them will say no. (01:15:31): And what I'm suggesting to you is that answer is going to change in the next two years.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为，如果你剖析一下什么是真正的协作，那么很多协作工作就是让人们获得正确的信息，掌握最真实的情况。这种问题现在已经有了显著改善。说实话，以前这部分工作简直糟透了。无论是状态报告，还是……我曾参与过这样的项目：文件被发送给我，我修改后再发送给我的上司，然后上司又转发给其他人……信息在组织内部不断传递，最终真相被埋没在某个角落，而人们却在添油加醋地解读事实。（01:14:05）：这种情况正在改变。但正如你所说，现在必须有人做出决策，有人要为之奋斗。这类讨论现在清晰多了，因为你掌握了真实情况，就减少了各种虚假信息。CEO可以直接问他们的代理：“情况如何？表现如何？客户真正想要什么？这对系统有何影响？我们是否真的需要调整产品来满足这些需求？” （01:14:33）：这样的对话可以进行，但现在人们可以基于真实数据展开讨论。如果你是一名产品经理，确实有自己的见解并想表达自己的观点，那就有了平台。因此，协作不会消失，但不会再有那么多戏剧性场面。我认为许多大公司确实存在这种戏剧性现象，而AI会消除这些问题。（01:14:59）：我不知道有多少产品经理会沉迷于这种戏剧性场面，但坦白说，大多数人都会说：“这简直是浪费时间。” 我敢打赌，如果你问你的产品经理：“你真的想当上司的上司吗？还是想过正常生活？不是为了薪资、声望，而是想参加无休止的会议？” 我敢打赌，大多数人都会说不想。（01:15:31）：我要告诉你的是，这种情况在未来两年内会发生变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really also interesting is, as much as this role is changing, engineering is changing even more. And what I feel like is that the engineers that will continue to thrive are basically going to become more PM-y, because the coding part is now going to be solved. And now it's just, "What should we build? Is this great? Is this the direction we want to go? What does success look like?" (01:15:59): So if you're like, " Oh shit, my job is changing," just imagine being an engineer right now and how crazy that must feel.
turns.zh: 真正有趣的是，虽然这个角色正在发生变化，但工程师的变化更大。我的感觉是，那些能够继续发展的工程师基本上会变得更像产品经理，因为编码部分现在已经解决了。现在的问题是：“我们应该开发什么？这个想法好吗？这是我们想要的方向吗？成功的样子是什么？” （01:15:59）：所以如果你觉得“天啊，我的职位要变了”，想象一下现在作为工程师的感觉吧，那得多崩溃啊。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. And I think the one advantage that engineers have is they think in systems, and they think about obsolescence more effectively. So I think that when you make a change, you have to decide, is this change going to be sustainable in the product that you're offering? I think an engineer has an edge there. (01:16:22): I think the other edge they have is, "I bet you we can build this to be more automated, to be simpler." I think those things-
turns.zh: 是的。我认为工程师的一个优势是，他们能从系统角度思考问题，更有效地考虑技术淘汰问题。因此，当你做出改变时，必须判断这种改变是否能在你提供的产品中持续下去？我认为工程师在这方面有优势。（01:16:22）：我认为他们还有另一个优势：“我敢打赌，我们可以把这个做得更自动化、更简单。” 我认为这些事情-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the minority goes there. Yeah.
turns.zh: 而少数人会选择这样做。是的。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. So I think that every one of us, the product person probably has a little bit of an edge in judgment and communication. The engineer's going to have a little bit of edge in the system scaling and how does this change affect folks? The designer's going to have a little bit of an edge with taste. And all of these things will still remain important. (01:16:50): And obviously people that have all of these will do better than those that have one or two, but the industry's more than safe, as evidenced by your report that there's more hiring. And I think it's going to grow. It's just different class of individual. This is what we're trying to communicate.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以我觉得我们每个人，产品人员可能在判断和沟通方面有一点优势。工程师在系统扩展以及这些变化如何影响用户方面会有一点优势。设计师在审美方面会有一点优势。所有这些能力都仍然很重要。（01:16:50）：显然，拥有所有这些能力的人会比只拥有一两种能力的人表现得更好，但行业发展得非常好，正如你的报告所示，招聘需求正在增加。我认为这个行业还会继续发展。这只不过是不同类型的个人。这一点正是我们试图传达的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The design piece is really surprising to me. The fact that this data show that the number of design roles is plateauing, and just how teams are just not valuing design as much as you think. You would think that design becomes much more important as the number of products grows exponentially, that it's a way to stand out, to build something really beautiful, and have a really thought-through experience. And it's interesting that that's not happening right now. (01:17:36): Also, just... I've been thinking about, there's no world where I'm a great designer. I can't just use AI and become a great designer. Unlike an engineer, maybe a PM, I could become a much better PM with AI. AI is knocking; it will do some cool stuff, but I'm not ever going to feel like I am a great designer now. (01:17:54): So it's really interesting that design isn't more successful right now with the rise of AI.
turns.zh: 设计方面让我很惊讶。数据显示设计岗位数量停滞不前，而团队对设计的重视程度远不如你想象的那样。你可能会认为随着产品数量呈指数级增长，设计会变得越来越重要，成为脱颖而出的方式，打造出美观且经过深思熟虑的体验。但有趣的是，目前情况并非如此。（01:17:36）：还有，我一直在思考，我永远不可能成为一名出色的设计师。我不能仅仅利用人工智能就成为一名出色的设计师。不像工程师，也许像产品经理，我可以借助人工智能成为更优秀的产品经理。人工智能正在兴起，它会做出一些很酷的事情，但我现在永远都不会觉得自己是一名出色的设计师。（01:17:54）：所以，在人工智能兴起的当下，设计没有变得更成功，这真的很有趣。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: And it might be that we just don't know what to make of design in this era. That might be a piece of it. The other piece might be just like there's product builders and then product information movers, and they're split up. I think that there are pixel generators and then there are tastemakers. And I worry that in design, maybe the industry itself conflates design with more production and not with taste. (01:18:32): And so I think there's a lot of companies that you would talk to, and even when they were hiring head of design, they were thinking more around, "We need more production." And great designers are much more tastemakers. And I think that is probably... that bias is entering into the hiring plans in this era that we have today.
turns.zh: 可能我们只是不了解在这个时代如何看待设计。这可能是原因之一。另一个原因可能是，产品开发者和产品信息推动者是分开的。我认为有像像素生成者和品味创造者这样的角色。我担心在设计领域，行业本身可能将设计与更多生产混为一谈，而非与品味相结合。（01:18:32）：所以，我认为有很多公司，当他们招聘设计主管时，更多地是在考虑：“我们需要更多的生产力。” 而优秀的设计师更多的是品味创造者。我认为这很可能……这种偏见正在影响我们当今的招聘计划。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a wild time we're living through, Nikhyl. Holy moly.
turns.zh: 尼基尔，我们正生活在一个疯狂的时代啊。天哪。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, isn't it funny that neither of us are operational? There are days when I'm like, "Man, am I so happy I have the time to work on this." And then other days that I think this is some of the most interesting... being operational right now is quite a ride. And so there's good and bad. (01:19:12): And COVID wasn't easy. There was a lot of challenges around working and seeing so much change. So there's always something, but this one's... everything's being questioned, including how you define joy, which I think is just absolutely fascinating.
turns.zh: 是啊，有趣的是我们俩都不是运营人员吗？有些日子我会想：“天哪，我真高兴有时间做这件事。” 而其他日子我又觉得现在做运营相当有趣。总有好有坏。（01:19:12）：新冠疫情也不容易。工作和见证如此多变化带来了很多挑战。所以总会有各种情况，但这次……一切都在被质疑，包括你如何定义快乐，我觉得这真的非常引人入胜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Chaos is a ladder, as Littlefinger famously said. Nikhyl, is there anything that we haven't covered? Anything else that you think is important for people to hear? Any other advice, anything you want to double down on before we wrap up and get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 正如小指头那句著名的台词所说：“混乱是一把梯子。” 尼基尔，还有什么我们没有涵盖到的吗？还有什么你认为对人们来说很重要、需要听到的吗？还有什么建议，或者在我们结束并进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你想再强调一下的吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I would just say that there's a lot of room to be optimistic right now, but you have to find it within yourself to recognize that there is a small period of change and exhaustion that's required to find that moment of joy. And I just urge everyone to find those reserves to get there, because once you do, it's infectious, but the longer you wait, the harder it is to cross that chasm. (01:20:17): And so I really want people to feel optimistic and find that moment of joy, but I also recognize that there is a lot of activation energy that it takes to get there. And so my hope is that you've... and there's a lot of people going through it. And so there's some safety in numbers here, but definitely I urge everyone to try their hand at rethinking their craft.
turns.zh: 我只想说，当下确实有很多值得乐观的地方，但你必须从内心深处认识到，要找到那个充满喜悦的时刻，就必须经历一段小小的变革与疲惫期。我真心希望大家能找到内在的力量去实现这一目标，因为一旦成功，这种积极的能量就会感染身边的人。但如果你拖延太久，跨越这道鸿沟就会愈发困难。（01:20:17）所以我真的希望人们能保持乐观，找到属于自己的快乐时刻，但我也清楚，要达成这一目标需要耗费巨大的能量。因此，我希望大家能努力重新审视自己的职业生涯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to be clear, you are seeing many people in the community doing well, enjoying this, thriving, this is possible.
turns.zh: 需要说明的是，你会看到社区里很多人做得很好，享受着这一切，蓬勃发展，这是完全有可能的。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, it's smiling exhaustion I see in my community. And before it was just exhaustion. So I take smiling exhaustion over exhaustion, but the pace is relentless. I don't have any... There's nothing I can say to sugarcoat that point.
turns.zh: 是啊，我在社区里看到的都是面带微笑的疲惫状态。以前他们只是单纯的疲惫。所以比起纯粹的疲惫，我更愿意接受这种带着微笑的疲惫，但生活节奏依然无情。我没法粉饰太平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a time to be alive. Well, Nikhyl, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 这真是令人振奋的时代。尼基尔，接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Go. Go for it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。尽情发挥吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常向他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: You know, Lenny, I'm not a reader. I hate to admit this, but I kind of vibe-code instead of most consumption of content right now. All of the reading I do is trying to stay up to date, and that was a casualty. So I don't listen to as many podcasts as I want to. I don't read as much as I want to, because I have so much information coming from the agents that I have deployed and all the stuff that's going on on Reddit and X and all that. (01:21:58): So I don't have a great set of book suggestions, not unlike all your other guests that are great at this. They read prolifically, and I just don't. I mean, I'll tell you, I read... I don't know how much I loved it, and I'll just leave it in here in case people are interested, but I read this book called James, which James is the story of Huckleberry Finn told from Jim's point of view. I thought that was absolutely fascinating, because anytime you take a classic and then you look at it through the eyes of someone else, and what you realize is that story is quite powerful, but very haunting. And when you read Huckleberry Finn, you're a kid. So the distinction between seeing the innocence, as not only the book was written from Twain's perspective, who was quite forward-thinking, by the way, but you remember you were a kid at the time, and now as an adult, you see the book from another angle. (01:23:04): I thought that was interesting. I don't know if I'd recommend it to your readers, but I thought I always look for things that I'm... unnatural stories that exist right in plain sight. So that was an example of that.
turns.zh: 你知道吗，伦尼，我不算个爱读书的人。我不太愿意承认，但现在我更多是通过“氛围代码”来获取信息。我读的书大多是用来保持资讯更新的，这方面有所牺牲。所以我听播客不像你希望的那么多，也不怎么阅读，因为我从部署的代理那里获取了大量信息，还有Reddit、X等平台上的各种内容。（01:21:58）所以我没有太多书单推荐，不像其他擅长这个的嘉宾。他们阅读量巨大，而我恰恰相反。我得告诉你，我读了本叫《詹姆斯》的书，詹姆斯是从吉姆的视角讲述《哈克贝利·费恩历险记》的故事。我觉得这本书非常引人入胜，因为每当你以不同视角解读经典作品时，会发现其内在的力量和令人不安的特质。当你读《哈克贝利·费恩》时，还是个孩子。所以你能区分出看到的纯真——这本书不仅出自吐温的视角，顺便说一句，他是个非常有远见的人——但你也会记得自己当时还是个孩子，而现在作为成年人，你从另一个角度看待这本书。（01:23:04）我觉得这很有趣。我不知道是否会推荐给你的读者，但我觉得自己总是在寻找那些存在于显而易见之处的非典型故事。这就是一个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think somebody else has actually recommended that book, so that's a second mention. Next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show? You've already shared some vibe-coding favorites to be in the background. Anything else?
turns.zh: 我想还有人推荐过这本书，所以这是第二次提及。下一个问题：你最近有没有喜欢的电影或电视剧？你之前分享过一些作为背景音乐的氛围代码音乐。还有别的推荐吗？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think everyone's talking about Paradise. I mean, if you haven't watched season one and season two, it's on Hulu.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，我觉得大家都在谈论《天堂》这部剧。要是你还没看过第一季和第二季，它在Hulu平台上能找到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, is season two out? I didn't realize that.
turns.zh: 哦，第二季上线了吗？我都不知道呢。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Season two is almost wrapping up, and I haven't watched season two yet. It's a little apocalyptic in nature, but it's absolute fascinating character drama about how people deal with very, very challenging times and what motivates individuals. (01:23:56): The other one that I really like is Lioness, which is on Paramount Plus. Lioness is a story really about a covert CIA group and how they deal with protecting security for America, and the importance and what it means to commit to a bigger cause. I thought that was a really well-written show. So both of those I recommend. (01:24:19): I do watch a ton of television, and as I mentioned, I vibe-code to certain shows. And these two I don't vibe-code to, because I have to pay attention.
turns.zh: 第二季快要完结了，可我还没看过第二季。这部剧有点末日题材的风格，但它绝对是一部引人入胜的人物剧，讲述人们如何应对极端艰难的时期，以及个人动机的驱动。（01:23:56）：另外一部我很喜欢的剧是《女战士》，播在派拉蒙+平台上。《女战士》讲的是一个CIA秘密小组如何为美国安全保驾护航的故事，强调了为更伟大事业奉献的重要性。我觉得这部剧剧本写得非常棒。所以这两部我都推荐。（01:24:19）：我确实看很多电视节目，正如我之前说的，我会根据个人喜好选择观看。这两部我没法边看边做其他事，因为得全神贯注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's the new bar if something's great.
turns.zh: 如果一部作品很棒，那这就是新的标准。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really love? Could be an app, could be some gadget, could be something else.
turns.zh: 好的。你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的新产品？可以是应用程序、电子设备，或者其他东西。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: My favorite product that I've discovered of late might be kind of obvious to a lot of folks, but I'm not a car guy, so I'll just start by saying that. Though I've enjoyed riding the newer electric cars, there's a large number of people that love cars, they love driving cars and talking about cars and repairing cars, just like the opposite of me. I just want my car to be super reliable. (01:25:10): And I've had a Tesla for a really long time, a Model S for just a long time, and I've had it since pretty much they came out with them. My daughter recently passed her driving exam, and because she passed her driving exam, one day my wife said, "Hey, we got to get her a car." And I was like, "We do?" I never actually connected the dots that she's going to need to drive a car. And I was like, "Well, when's she going to go?" And eventually I'm like, "Okay, maybe we should buy our car, but she's not going to drive that much. Maybe I should use this as an opportunity to upgrade my car." (01:25:44): And so I drove the latest Teslas that are out there, the ones with the self-driving. And the self-driving works quite well, just to be clear. I mean, I have it now for the last month, and about 95% of the time I self-drive. But the most interesting thing is I had no idea that I actually have mild anxiety when I drive that goes away when I self-drive, and I had no idea. And my wife noticed it when we were driving up to the mountains one day, and it was crazy snowing, and I'm like, "We're going to do it." And she's like, "You are so anxious when you drive." And I'm like, "I am?" (01:26:22): Because, Lenny, I've been driving since I was 14 years old, because I grew up in Kansas. And so I passed the test when I was 14. So I've been driving literally for nearly 40 years, and I had no idea, as I've gotten older, that this pressing a button and going places is just so awesome. (01:26:39): So anyway, the reason why that experience is interesting, yeah, there's the tech and all that, it's just like I look for ways to reduce my anxiety. Anything that causes anxiety, I try to eliminate at this point in my life, and this is one of them. So that's a cool product for me.
turns.zh: 我最近发现的最喜欢的产品，可能对很多人来说并不意外，但我对车一窍不通，所以先说一句。虽然我也喜欢开新款电动车，但大多数爱车人士热爱驾驶、谈论汽车、修理汽车，简直与我南辕北辙。我只希望自己的车能超可靠。（01:25:10）：我用特斯拉 Model S 已经很久了，几乎从它上市就开始用了。最近我女儿通过了驾照考试，妻子说得突然：“得给她买辆车。”我当时还说：“买车？”完全没意识到她以后要开车。又问：“那她多久能开车啊？”最后我决定：“好吧，或许该换辆车了，但她又不会常开。”（01:25:44）：于是我试了最新款的自动驾驶特斯拉。说实话，自动驾驶功能确实很棒。过去一个月里，我95%的时间都是自动驾驶。但最有趣的是，我完全没意识到自己开车时会感到焦虑，而自动驾驶能消除这种焦虑。某天开车去山上时，雪下得特别大，我妻子说：“你太紧张了。” 我说：“紧张？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that as a rule. I've also become all in on self-driving. I've had a Tesla for a long time, from the beginnings of their explorations into self-driving, and it was always just like, "I don't know, this is scary." And now it's the opposite. My wife prefers I self-drive. Even though I drive well, she just feels safer when the self-driving is on. (01:27:13): And there's this... in the actual settings, they give you a stat of what percentage you're driving is self-driving, and they noted it's since 14.2, I think was the release on like that. So that was the release that everyone started being like, "Wow, it's actually very good now." And I don't think a lot of people realize that it's actually incredibly good. I haven't had a single concerning moment.
turns.zh: 我对此深有体会。说实话，我现在完全沉浸在自动驾驶的乐趣中。从 14 岁在堪萨斯州拿驾照开始，我就一直在开车。如今 40 年过去了，才发现按下按钮就能自动驾驶是多么神奇的体验。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: This is one of those examples in product where so many people try the previous versions that when you then tell your friend... a lot of people have Teslas, obviously in California but across the world, when you tell your friends, a lot of people are like, "Oh yeah, I tried it and I turned it off." So I think Tesla's got this unusual challenge of getting people to turn it back on. And obviously the newer hardware is better than the older one, and the newest software. (01:27:57): But once you go through one experience, it can be hard to convince someone to try it again, and that's an adage in product and certainly applies here.
turns.zh: 这是产品领域的一个典型例子，太多人体验过旧版本，以至于当你向朋友推荐时……很多人会说：“哦，对，我试过但后来关掉了。”所以我觉得特斯拉面临一个特殊挑战——要让用户重新启用这项功能。显然，新硬件比旧硬件更出色，新软件也更先进。（01:27:57）但一旦用户有过糟糕体验，就很难说服他们再尝试一次。这在产品领域是个铁律，特斯拉的案例也充分印证了这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a downside of releasing early and often sometimes people just have this memory of what it might be. I feel like it's like Uber where you have to just start hearing about it from your friends telling you, "Hey, I'm doing this thing." I'm like, "Wait, really? I guess I should try it."
turns.zh: 提前发布产品有时会带来负面影响，用户会对产品形成刻板印象。比如优步（Uber）刚起步时，大家都是从朋友口中听说这项服务的，朋友会说：“嘿，我正在用这个功能。”然后你会说：“等等，真的吗？看来我也该试试。”

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Here's a Tesla suggestion for anyone who's listening is Lenny and I should be able to gift 30 days free to our friends of self-driving, people that have turned it off, because the referral of that plus the endorsement allows people to experience it for free and then they can get their monthly subscription.
turns.zh: 我给听众的建议是，伦尼（Lenny）和我应该能给朋友送上30天免费自动驾驶体验券。这些用户曾关闭过自动驾驶功能，通过口口相传和推荐，让他们免费体验后再订阅月费服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great idea.
turns.zh: 好主意。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: That viral plus enablement I think is a growth technique that they can have for free from us.
turns.zh: 这种病毒式传播加推荐机制，是我们能免费为他们提供的增长策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good idea. By the way, I love Mad Max mode. I love just the personality of the stuff just... Are you a hurry mode guy or are you a standard mode guy?
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便说一句，我超爱“疯狂模式”。我喜欢这种产品个性，嗯……你喜欢“急躁模式”还是“标准模式”？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I flip between them, but I do feel like and I'm hoping that the new release of the software keeps us in the lane. I don't love it changing lanes, but it's-
turns.zh: 我两个模式都切换，但我希望新版软件能让我们保持在正确车道上。不喜欢它随意变道，但……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, like where it's trying to hurry a little bit?
turns.zh: 哦，比如它想快点变道？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: Yeah, I wish I could just get it to go at a normal speed, but also don't change lanes because I just don't like moving around.
turns.zh: 是啊，我希望能让它保持正常速度行驶，同时不变道，因为我不喜欢频繁切换车道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Next question. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 好的。下个问题。你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，在工作或生活中经常回味的？

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: My high school quote in my yearbook still is my motto, which is, "Genius is 1% inspiration, 99% perspiration," by Albert Einstein. It's something that even at an early age... and it's not about genius being capital G. I wasn't a New York comment. It was more like hard work is really what matters in life. (01:29:48): What's interesting is, if you read that quote, "Genius is 1% inspiration, 99% perspiration," through the lens of AI, it's absolutely fascinating, because it turns out the AI will do the perspiration quite literally.
turns.zh: 我高中年册上的那句话至今仍是我的座右铭：“天才的1%是灵感，99%是汗水”，出自阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦。这句话即使在年少时就深深触动我……这里的“天才”不是字面意义上的天才。我可不是纽约评论家，而是强调勤奋才是人生真谛。（01:29:48）有趣的是，如果从AI的视角解读这句话，“天才的1%是灵感，99%是汗水”，简直令人惊叹，因为AI确实会非常字面地去“挥洒汗水”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Unlimited perspiration.
turns.zh: 无限挥洒汗水。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: So I think what we're leaning towards is we all need to... we're moving to a world where we're all going to be inspired, and it's the inspired individuals in all of us that will essentially continue to proliferate. And don't worry about the perspiration, but recognize that it is the perspiration that is a necessity to make things go. (01:30:27): Anyway, I think it's an interesting quote, especially in today's era.
turns.zh: 所以我认为我们的方向应该是，我们都需要……向着一个所有人都充满灵感的世界前进，而我们每个人内心的灵感种子必将继续蓬勃生长。别担心汗水部分，要明白正是汗水才让一切得以运转。（01:30:27）总之，这句话很值得深思，尤其在当今时代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. People may have noticed that we've started collaborating on your podcast and your newsletter. It's such an underappreciated, under... I don't know, seen thing that you do. This podcast, this newsletter, it fills such a gap in the content out there around product building, of just very tactical, important, non-sugar-coated career advice for people in product. (01:30:57): And what I love about it is it's not AI most of the time. In spite of this conversation we just had, it's very much like, "Here's stuff you need to know that is not flashy and shiny, AI, AI, AI, all the time." So I want to give you a chance just to tell people about the podcast, the newsletter, what ideas, where they can find it.
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。大家可能已经注意到，我们开始在你的播客和通讯上进行合作了。你所做的事情太不被重视、太被低估了……我不知道该怎么形容。你的播客和通讯填补了产品构建领域内容的空白，为产品从业者提供了非常实用、重要且直言不讳的职业建议。（01:30:57）：我特别喜欢的一点是，大多数时候内容都不是关于AI的。尽管我们刚刚进行了这场对话，但大部分内容都是：“这里有一些你需要知道的东西，不花哨也不浮华，不是AI、AI、AI、AI、AI。” 所以我想给你一个机会，让大家了解一下播客和通讯的内容、理念，以及哪里可以找到它们。

turns.speaker: Nikhyl Singhal
turns.en: I started this property called Skip because I really felt that there was a dearth of content from operators sharing best practices with emerging operators. And the idea was, look, I had been a founder before, I'd been an executive before, and I wanted to be in a position where I can say, "Hey, this is exactly what I experienced, and this might apply to you." And I noticed that most of the podcasts and the content out there were from folks that hadn't spent as much time in operating, more time in content, and I was kind of the opposite. (01:31:51): Then I started building this community that I spoke about last time, which was about 20-30 at the time. Now it's over 125 head of product, who are all these builders, top of their game, and reinventing what product management looked like. And our goal is to collectively share our wisdom as operators to help people advance in career. And that calling is probably more important now than ever, as everything's changing. (01:32:19): And so one of the things that we're launching next month, but by the time that we end up launching this episode, is something called Skip.help, where we have agents that have been trained on about 50 of our community leaders. And so you can go and ask a question. It might be preparing for an interview, it might be a question around navigating your current environment. It might even be, "How do I build a chief of staff app?" And 50 of us, not just me, will respond. And this is powered by our friends over at Superme, which is a great startup that actually, by having these agents, you get the wisdom of the crowds. (01:32:58): And so those are the things that I love. And obviously the community itself is a very curated group, and there's an infinite wait list, a lot of people want to be in. And I'm only growing it slowly because I want to maintain trust. But I do have this mailing list called Skip.coach, where we share our wisdom to a broader audience. (01:33:19): I know I've gotten every single domain name that starts with Skip. Skip community, Skip shows, my podcast, Skip coach, Skip help. But anyway, go to any of them and you can triangulate to all of them. I always appreciate, Lenny, your support and your help in building this property with me. So it's been great. turns.zh: 我创办了名为Skip的平台，因为我真的觉得，运营者之间分享最佳实践的优质内容太少了。我的想法是，看，我以前是创始人，后来是高管，现在我想处于这样一个位置："嘿，这就是我的亲身经历，或许对你也适用。" 我注意到，大多数播客和现有内容都来自那些没有花太多时间在运营上、而更多时间在内容创作上的人，而我恰恰相反。（01:31:51）：然后我开始建立上次提到的社区，当时大约有20-30人。现在已经有超过125位产品负责人加入，他们都是顶尖的从业者，正在重塑产品管理的面貌。我们的目标是作为运营者集体分享智慧，帮助人们在职业上取得进步。在一切都在变化的当下，我们的使命比以往任何时候都更加重要。（01:32:19）：所以下个月我们将推出一个新项目，但到本期节目结束时，我们将正式上线一个叫Skip.help的平台。我们有经过培训的客服人员，他们来自我们的社区领导团队中的约50人。你可以去那里提问。可能是为面试做准备，可能是关于如何应对当前环境的问题，甚至可能是"如何开发一个参谋长应用程序？" 我们将有50人（不只是我）来回复这些问题。这个平台由我们的合作伙伴Superme提供支持，这是一家很棒的初创公司，通过这些客服人员，你能获得群体的智慧。（01:32:58）：这些都是我喜欢的地方。显然，社区本身是一个精心筛选的群体，等待名单长得离谱，很多人都想加入。我只会慢慢扩大规模，因为我希望保持信任。但我确实有一个名为Skip.coach的邮件列表，我们在那里向更广泛的受众分享智慧。（01:33:19）：我知道我注册了所有以Skip开头的域名。Skip社区、Skip节目、我的播客、Skip coach、Skip help。但无论如何，访问其中任何一个，你都可以链接到所有平台。我一直很感激，Lenny，你的支持和与我共同打造这个平台的帮助。真的很棒。当我加入时，我想我还没有开始做我的播客，现在我即将迎来第50期节目，你显然已经超过300期了。所以看到事情如何变化、如何发生真的很有趣。所以一切都很棒。
